llama.origin: The llama (Lama glama) is a domestic South American camelid of the Andean highlands. Mitochondrial and microsatellite analysis by Kadwell and colleagues (2001) supports descent of the llama from the guanaco (Lama guanicoe), whereas the alpaca traces mainly to the vicuna and was proposed for reclassification as Vicugna pacos. The same study found extensive two-way hybridization between the domestic forms, so a fleece sold as llama may carry mixed ancestry. Because llamas have been bred for several purposes, fleece fineness and guard-hair content vary widely between animals and herds.
llama.structure: Llama fleece is double-coated. Britannica describes coarse guard hairs of the protective outer coat as making up roughly 20 percent of the fleece, with the rest a short, crimped insulating undercoat. Reported undercoat diameters span about 20 to 40 microns, a broader and on average coarser range than typical alpaca. Both fractions are alpha-keratin fibers with a cuticle of thin scales over a cortex. The decisive structural variable is the medulla, which camelid fiber laboratories classify as absent, fragmented, discontinuous, continuous or strongly medullated. Medullated fibers resist bending and compression, so they feel stiffer and can dye differently, which makes the medullated share a central quality measure.
llama.process: Harvest is by shearing, followed by skirting to remove coarse leg, neck and belly hair and debris. Because guard hair and undercoat differ in diameter and stiffness, quality yarn requires dehairing, either by hand picking or on mechanical dehairing lines of the kind used for cashmere, which exploit differences in fiber length and rigidity. The separated undercoat is scoured, carded and spun on the woollen or worsted route. The coarse fraction is not waste: it can be spun into strong yarn for rugs, rope and cordage. Sorting by natural color is common because much llama yarn is sold undyed.
llama.performance: Dehaired llama undercoat behaves like other fine keratin fibers: it absorbs water vapor, stays warm when slightly damp, and chars and self-extinguishes rather than melting. Its crimp gives loft, but garments with residual guard hair feel prickly, because stiff fibers above roughly 30 microns (the threshold used in the comfort factor measure) press into the skin. This is why dehairing quality matters more than the animal name. Acid dyes and other wool dye classes bind to the amino groups of keratin, although strongly medullated fibers can dye unevenly. Like all protein fibers, llama is attacked by clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae and weakened by alkaline detergents.
llama.identify: Burn tests are indicative only and should be done with care: llama smolders, smells of burning hair and leaves a crushable black ash, like any hair fiber. Microscopy shows scaled keratin fibers with a medulla in many of them; projection microscopy prepared under IWTO-8 and newer automated image systems measure mean diameter and classify medullation. Visual separation of llama from alpaca is unreliable, so species claims in a finished product need DNA or protein-based laboratory methods, which a 2023 review of analytical methods for fine animal fibers surveys.
llama.labeling: In the United States the Wool Products Labeling Act of 1939 includes llama among the specialty fibers that may fall within the statutory definition of wool, and the name of the specialty fiber may be used in place of the word wool when its percentage is stated. The FTC rule at 16 CFR 303.6 expressly excludes llama from the catch-all term fur fiber. In the European Union, Annex I of Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 lists llama among the named fine animal hairs, which may be followed or not by the word wool or hair. No llama-specific welfare standard was identified in this review.
llama.past: Kadwell and colleagues note that the ancestry of domestic South American camelids has been contested because of hybridization, difficulties in archaeological interpretation and near extirpation of the domestic herds during the Spanish conquest. Their genetic results placed the llama with the guanaco lineage and cited earlier research dating alpaca domestication to about 6,000 to 7,000 years before present in the Peruvian Andes. The llama's role as the larger pack animal helps explain why many herds were not selected primarily for fine fleece. Modern breeding programs and fiber laboratories now use diameter and medullation measurements, rather than appearance alone, to grade llama and alpaca fleeces.
